title: Why 1746 happened
hookLine: a governor's minister, grieving his brother, turned on the Sikhs, and the loss that followed is remembered as the small holocaust

cards: A body is carried into Lahore. The dead man is Jaspat Rai, an official who rode out against a Sikh band and was killed in the fighting. His brother, Lakhpat Rai, is a minister at the governor's court.
Tradition says Lakhpat Rai took off his turban, threw it down, and swore he would not put it on again until he had wiped the Sikhs out. One man's grief. Soon it had an army behind it.
This path has already walked through what happened next, the small holocaust; today asks why.

teach.b: The grief was real. Lakhpat Rai lost his brother. But watch what the grief turned into.
Tradition says he didn't stop at the fighters: Sikhs living quietly in Lahore were rounded up.

Tradition says he went further still: he ordered that the Sikh scriptures not be read, and even that the word gur, which means the Guru but is also the Punjabi word for brown sugar, not be spoken in the city.

People were told to call the sugar something else. A man's sorrow had grown into a war on a whole people, down to a word in the market. The army marched, and the loss that followed is remembered as the Chhota Ghallughara.
Now set beside that a word from the very first line of Sikh scripture, describing God: nirvair.

Without hate, without enmity. And Guru Arjan in the Granth, in paraphrase: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone. That line sits in the same scripture the minister tried to silence.
And look at how the story is kept. The Ardas, the prayer said at the end of gurdwara gatherings, remembers those who gave their lives for the faith. It remembers them; it doesn't curse anyone.
The names of the dead are carried; the hatred isn't. Grief is not the danger. Grief is what love does when someone is taken.
The danger is the moment grief decides someone must pay, and keeps widening the circle of who that someone is.
Lakhpat Rai's story shows that moment; the Sikh way of remembering it shows grief without hate.

how: Sikhs remember those who died in the eighteenth-century persecutions in the Ardas, the prayer said at the close of gurdwara gatherings, which honors the martyrs without cursing anyone.

o: without rest, always moving from place to place
without sorrow, untouched by loss or grief
without hate, without enmity toward anyone

games.q: the story behind the year — tap the pairs.
p: the brother killed in a clash

s: tradition says even the word gur was banned in Lahore
gur means the Guru and also brown sugar, and people were told to call the sugar something else.
Sikhs tell this story to keep a curse on the people who did it
the Ardas remembers those who died. it doesn't curse anyone.
the persecution was aimed only at the band that killed Jaspat Rai
tradition says it widened to Sikhs living quietly in Lahore, and then to a whole people.

games.q: you're Lakhpat Rai. your brother has just been killed in a fight with a Sikh band. what do you do?
o: mourn him, and leave it there.
punish only the men who fought him.
swear to wipe out every Sikh.
games.why: tradition says he threw down his turban and vowed to destroy the Sikhs, and his grief widened into a persecution of a whole people.

practice: Bring to mind a loss, yours or a wrong done to someone you love, one you can hold for two minutes, and let the sadness be there.
If a wish that someone would pay rides along with it, set it gently apart, like a heavy bag beside you: keep the love, loosen the grip on the blame. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: nirvair, without hate. Tradition says a minister's grief for his brother became a vow of revenge against a whole people, even though the opening line of Sikh scripture names God this way.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nirvair, without hate or enmity, a word from the opening line of the Guru Granth Sahib describing God.

carryVoice: Your line: grief without hate. Sorrow can stay without the circle of blame growing. See you tomorrow.
